blocks.text: We can increase the flow velocity of water in a rubber pipe by squeezing it. When we squeeze the rubber pipe we decrease the cross-sectional area through which the water flows. According to the equation of continuity, A1 v1 = A2 v2 ... (5.18), where A is the cross-sectional area and v the flow velocity. By decreasing the cross-sectional area (A2 less than A1) the velocity of the water (v2) must increase to maintain the same flow rate. Therefore squeezing the rubber pipe increases the flow velocity of water.

blocks.prompt: A garden hose is squeezed to a quarter of its opening; what happens to the water speed and to the volume delivered per second?
blocks.explanation: The speed becomes four times greater, since A v is constant, while the volume delivered per second is unchanged (ignoring the small extra resistance of the narrowed nozzle).

items: Squeezing a rubber pipe reduces A, so by A1 v1 = A2 v2 the water speeds up; the flow rate stays the same.
